title: Hundreds of Mundane AI Apps Are Hiding Sexually Abusive Deepfake Features
gist: A Wired investigation found a network of 400+ domains and apps, apparently run by Chinese developers and Hong Kong entity KeLing Technology Limited, that pose as benign AI apps but load hidden sexual deepfake interfaces, promoted by tens of thousands of Meta ads and distributed via Apple and Google app stores despite their policies. Platforms removed many only after being contacted.

insights.claim: Wired found a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps, posing as services like pet portraits, language tuition and workout coaching, that stealthily load a web interface for generating explicit AI sexual images and videos from uploaded photos.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Scale and disguise defeat app-store review.
insights.quote: A WIRED investigation found the app is part of a network of more than 400 connected domains and apps

insights.claim: On each download the app calls a server with information such as origin, language and a unique identifier, and the server decides whether to show benign or explicit content; one trigger appears to be installing after clicking a Meta ad.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Cloaking lets malicious apps pass store review.

insights.claim: A JavaScript bundle on the sites exposes a configuration list of the whole network's domains, app package details, encryption keys and Facebook ad trackers.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Operational security failures enabled researchers to map the network.
insights.quote: They contained this giant configuration list of other domains with different encryption keys

insights.claim: Apps began appearing at the end of 2025, spiking in spring 2026 with around 30 apps-websites registered weekly; 27 were live on Google Play in September with over 350,000 combined downloads, many rated suitable for all ages.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Sustained industrial-scale abuse of app distribution.

insights.claim: DiffAI, created December 2025, had more than 100,000 Play Store downloads before removal; a user review said it contained CSAM templates and performed no age verification.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Regulatory and liability exposure for platform operators.

insights.claim: The explicit interface sells 'diamonds' to generate content, and a late-September notice announced a new model called Veyra.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: The operation monetizes via in-app purchases and payments.

insights.claim: Apple removed 19 apps, including Viefur, after WIRED's inquiry; it said the apps complied when reviewed, then developers swapped the website content, and that it has suspended tens of thousands of apps for such bait-and-switch tactics over the last year.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Post-approval content swaps are a structural app-review gap.

insights.claim: Google removed most of the apps before being contacted but did not respond to WIRED's request for comment; portions of the network were reported by Danish journalists in September.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Enforcement is reactive to press, not proactive.

insights.claim: Meta says it banned KeLing Technology Limited from advertising in 2025 after it failed to comply with a cease and desist, and after WIRED's report it acted against 11,600 ad accounts, 4,700 business pages, 5,200 users and 15,000 pages and blocked 209 apps.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Scale of Meta's remediation reveals the size of the problem.

insights.claim: Researchers say tens of thousands of explicit deepfake ads tied to the network ran on Meta's platforms this year, using fake payer names, and similar ads and apps were still being published as reporting finished.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Regulatory investigations into ad-platform deepfake enforcement are ongoing worldwide.

insights.claim: Bouchaud described the operation as organized and commercial, expecting enforcement not to catch up, and says it hasn't so far.
insights.speaker: Paul Bouchaud
insights.so_what: Adversaries view platform enforcement as a cost of doing business.
insights.quote: They don’t expect enforcement to catch up, and so far it hasn’t.

insights.claim: Katie Paul of the Tech Transparency Project says tech companies must answer where money from the apps goes and how operators repeatedly bypass moderation systems.
insights.speaker: Katie Paul
insights.so_what: Payment rails (Apple Pay, Google Pay) are an emerging pressure point.

insights.claim: Researchers attribute the network to Chinese developers and Hong Kong-registered KeLing Technology Limited based on Chinese hosting, Chinese-language code comments, and Chinese video editing watermarks in ads.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess

insights.claim: After WIRED made contact, the KeLing name was erased from some websites and social channels, suggesting active concealment.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
